Science fiction is the realm of endless creativity. It's the genre that has greatly influenced popular culture, delivering some of our most exciting stories and forever pushing the limits of storytelling to the absolute extremes. Sci-fi fascinated us long before the age of filmmaking really launched its popularity into the stratosphere.

We've been blessed over the last few centuries with compelling sci-fi literature. The greatest, most influential, and inspiring of these iconic novels from this genre have gone on to have a commanding presence in storytelling and even in cinema. There are notable classics that are essential, timeless even, and deserve all the praise we give them. From a beloved intergalactic adventure comedy to one of the most powerful space epics of all time, these are essential sci-fi books you need to read at least once.

blocks.c: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy - 1979

blocks.x: Starting off is The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, a beloved sci-fi comedy novel based on a radio series of the same name by Douglas Adams. A hilarious adventure spanning multiple unique worlds, it's a delightful blast that devoted sci-fi lovers have enjoyed for nearly half a century now. It follows the misadventures of Arthur Dent, the last man alive after Earth's cataclysmic destruction, as he goes exploring the most absurd reaches of outer space with his alien best friend Ford Perfect.

Upon publication, The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy became an instant sci-fi classic, one that readers loved so much that it spawned an equally successful book series and even a cult favorite film adaptation in 2005 starring Martin Freeman as Dent. It blends uproarious comedy with thrilling sci-fi adventures, culminating in an endlessly fun story that's worth reading from front to back.

blocks.c: Book cover to John W. Campbell's 'Who Goes There?'

blocks.x: Written by one of the most influential science fiction authors to ever live, John W. Campbell, comes the groundbreaking novella Who Goes There?, a masterclass in storytelling. This 1938 classic revolutionized the sci-fi horror genre, popularizing it with its frighteningly creative tale that perfectly balanced the two. It tells of an American research team under attack in their isolated outpost in Antarctica by a menacing shapeshifting alien organism that is able to disguise itself as any of them.

It's nearly 230 pages of perfect suspense and terror, creating an uneasy reading experience. Not to mention, it hits the ground running in its first ten pages, gripping readers immediately with its great character introductions, and it subtly teases what horrors await them later in the story. It not only influenced the genre in literature, it also impacted cinema as well, as its two notable film adaptations, 1954's The Thing From Another World and John Carpenter's 1982 classic The Thing, became dominant forces in pop culture, even becoming recognized as some of the best horror movies ever created. Overall, Campbell's novel is a trailblazer that sci-fi fans can truly appreciate.

blocks.c: The book cover of William Gibson's 'Neuromancer'

blocks.x: An icon of the sci-fi genre that birthed the modern cyberpunk aesthetic, author William Gibson's 1984 award-winning novel Neuromancer is a staple that any sci-fi enthusiast has at least heard about. A kick-ass tale full of high-stakes action, heist-adventure excitement, and AI rampant mayhem, it follows a skilled but disgraced hacker named Case as he's recruited to help merge two very powerful artificial entities into a super-intelligence.

Neuromancer is a striking novel with excellently explored themes about corporate supremacy, identity and body loss, and moral uncertainty advancing artifical intelligence. In short, it's an essential read that has remained consistently popular since its publication. It not only revolutionized the cyberpunk look and defined it for decades, but also became a benchmark for other A.I. related thrillers, cementing itself as a timelessly inspired masterpiece.

One of the eeriest sci-fi dystopian groundbreakers of all time, George Orwell's 1984 has kept readers paranoid for decades. It's a revolutionary tale that brought thought-provoking themes of totalitarianism and suppression to the frightening realm of possibility. The story is set in an alternate future where an endless war devastating the planet has caused Great Britain to form a totalitarian state, causing a dictatorial leader, Big Brother, to rule with an iron fist. In the wake of the government's complete control over everyone, one man, Winston Smith, slowly begins to secretly rebel against the system.

It's one of the most impactful satires in all literature, an absolutely creative marvel that warns us about oppression and mass surveillance, and remains just as relevant and terrifying now as it was when it was released in 1949. It's an absolute must-read for more than just sci-fi fans, as it's perfectly structured and has a powerful message that carries with it much urgency.

blocks.c: The cover art for Philip K. Dick's 'Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?'

blocks.x: From renowned sci-fi novelist Philip K. Dick comes his legendary masterpiece, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?. This profound and masterful story laid the groundwork for the cyberpunk sci-fi genre, laying down the foundation that so many novels, movies, and video games would build from. Set in the post-apocalyptic future of San Francisco, reclusive bounty hunter Rick Deckard is tasked with killing six rouge androids running loose in the city that have started forming their own independent identities.

Packed with sharp writing, a brilliant pace, and some of the most thought-provoking themes ever told in a book, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? is an undeniable staple of the genre that has remained consistently relevant and timeless over the years. It, of course, became the basis for Ridley Scott's 1982 groundbreaking film Blade Runner, one of cinema's most inspiring sci-fi classics. Overall, this is one novel no one who enjoys reading can skip.

blocks.c: Book cover of H.G. Wells' 'The War of the Worlds'

blocks.x: The most pioneering sci-fi alien invasion novel of all time deserves a notable mention on this list. Created by the legendary English author H. G. Wells, The War of the Worlds made its way into history, becoming a tremendous source of influence that is still present in storytelling today, even more than one hundred years after its publication. It tells the timeless story of alien invaders from Mars coming to strip Earth of its natural resources, leaving the dwindling human survivors to figure out a way to stop them.

It's perhaps the most adapted story in film history, aside from one more iconic novel mentioned below. The War of the Worlds was retold in an iconic Orson Welles radio play, countless imitators, and a whole list of adaptations. It's safe to say it inspired generations of storytellers and sci-fi fans. It popularized the idea of an alien invasion, which readers and movie lovers can't seem to get enough of these days. Honestly, it's an essential read for everyone.

All hail to the quintessential sci-fi horror novel Frankenstein, written by the unforgettable Mary Shelley in 1818. A renowned masterpiece, responsible for breaking the limits of storytelling, this timeless Gothic novel helped mold the science fiction and horror genres into what we know them today. It's a dark tale of loss, revenge, and human ambition resulting in destruction as it tells the tragedy of the brilliant scientist Dr. Victor Frankenstein as he breaks the rules of nature by resurrecting an unstable being from dead tissue, only to have his life destroyed by the creature once he rejects it.

It can't be overstated how utterly flawless and impactful this novel is. It's strikingly creative with its story and tragic themes about creation and ambition. The characters became synonymous with horror, especially the Monster, who gained new life and an extra dose of popularity among audiences thanks to the invention of film in the early 20th century. Today, it is one of the most adapted novels in cinema history, and continues to influence this art form. There is no doubt about it; sci-fi would never have been the same without Shelley's impeccable classic.

blocks.c: Dune by Frank Herbert book cover.

blocks.x: At the end of the day, one iconic sci-fi book stands above all the rest as the ultimate classic that other novels bow their heads to. That is Frank Herbert's landmark masterpiece, Dune, published in 1965. An absolute achievement that revolutionized sci-fi storytelling, this epic otherworldly adventure takes readers on a captivating journey, following the rise of the charismatic chosen one, Paul Atreides, as he leads a desert world's people in his holy war against an intergalactic empire that betrayed his noble house.

Think about it: Without Dune, we'd likely never have had Star Wars, The Matrix, Alien, or even 2001: A Space Odyssey without its influential storytelling. Frank Herbert created a blueprint that fundamentally reshaped science fiction, turning it into a limitless potential for storytellers to think bigger and more creatively. It honestly can't go unnoticed when mentioning the most influential sci-fi novels of all time these days, and for that, it honorably takes the final spot on this list.
